Keywords: stdio transport, sse transport, streamable http, mcp transport
Guidance: stdio is simplest for local single-client tools (like Claude Desktop/Code launching a subprocess), but a server meant to be shared across multiple remote clients needs SSE/Streamable HTTP instead.
Do: Use stdio for local single-process integrations; use Streamable HTTP (or SSE) for servers that need to be reachable remotely or by multiple concurrent clients.
Don't: Build a multi-tenant remote MCP server on stdio transport, which assumes a single local process pair.

Keywords: tool schema, tool description, parameter description, mcp tool design
Guidance: A vague tool description ('does stuff with data') gives the calling model no basis to decide when to use it correctly or what parameters actually mean.
Do: Write specific, unambiguous tool descriptions and per-parameter descriptions, including what the tool does NOT do if that's likely to be confused.
Don't: Ship an MCP tool with a one-word name and no description, relying on the model to infer its purpose.
Example: {'name': 'search_orders', 'description': 'Search orders by customer email or order ID. Does not search product catalog.'}

Keywords: mcp auth, oauth, server authentication, unauthenticated server
Guidance: Running a remote MCP server with no authentication means anyone who can reach the endpoint can invoke its tools, which is especially dangerous for tools with write/destructive side effects.
Do: Implement OAuth (or another auth mechanism per the MCP spec) for any MCP server reachable over the network, especially ones with side-effecting tools.
Don't: Expose a remote MCP server with write-capable tools and no authentication on a network-reachable endpoint.

Keywords: mcp resource, mcp tool, read vs action, resource uri
Guidance: Modeling read-only reference data as a tool call (instead of a Resource) makes it harder for clients to cache, subscribe to updates, or present it outside the model's tool-call loop.
Do: Use Resources for addressable, primarily-read data and Tools for actions/computations with side effects or dynamic parameters.
Don't: Expose all read-only data through tool calls instead of using Resources, losing addressability and caching benefits.

Keywords: tool error response, isError, mcp error handling
Guidance: Returning a raw exception stack trace (or silently returning empty/null on failure) as a tool result gives the calling model no actionable signal to recover or explain the failure to the user.
Do: Return structured error responses (isError: true with a clear message) so the model can reason about and communicate the failure appropriately.
Don't: Let unhandled exceptions in a tool handler propagate as an opaque transport-level error with no actionable message.

Keywords: rate limiting, backoff, external api quota, mcp server reliability
Guidance: An MCP tool that wraps an external API with no rate limiting or backoff can get the server's credentials throttled or banned when a model calls it in a tight loop.
Do: Implement rate limiting/backoff inside tool handlers that wrap external APIs, and surface clear rate-limit errors back to the model.
Don't: Let an MCP tool call an external API with no rate limiting, allowing a runaway agent loop to exhaust the quota.
Example: time.sleep(backoff_seconds)  # before retrying a rate-limited external call

Keywords: server registration, mcp config, claude_desktop_config, server manifest
Guidance: Hand-editing multiple client configuration files to register the same MCP server (once per client/machine) drifts out of sync and makes it easy to point different clients at different server versions.
Do: Maintain a single source-of-truth server manifest/config and script its registration across clients rather than hand-editing each config file.
Don't: Hand-edit claude_desktop_config.json (or equivalent) separately on every machine with no shared source of truth for server config.

Keywords: tool permissions, least privilege, destructive tool, scoped access
Guidance: Exposing a broad database-admin-level tool (arbitrary SQL execution) when the actual use case only needs read-only querying gives any calling model far more capability than the task requires.
Do: Scope tools narrowly to the actual required operations (e.g. a parameterized read-only query tool) rather than exposing a general-purpose escape hatch.
Don't: Expose a generic 'run_sql' tool with full read/write database access when the use case only needs read-only lookups.
Example: {'name': 'get_customer_orders', 'description': 'Read-only lookup of orders for a given customer ID.'}

Keywords: large tool output, context window, result truncation
Guidance: Returning an entire unfiltered database table or full document as a tool result can blow past the model's context window in one call and drown out relevant information.
Do: Paginate, filter, or summarize large tool results server-side, and let the model request more detail explicitly if needed.
Don't: Return an entire multi-thousand-row table as raw tool output for a query that needed one filtered row.
Example: {'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Showing 10 of 4213 results. Use offset param for more.'}]}

Keywords: idempotent tool, retry safety, side effect, duplicate action
Guidance: A tool that isn't idempotent (like 'create_invoice') can produce duplicate side effects if a client retries after an ambiguous timeout or transport error.
Do: Design side-effecting tools to accept an idempotency key or to check-before-act, so retries after ambiguous failures are safe.
Don't: Build a side-effecting tool with no idempotency guarantee, relying on the calling agent to never retry.

Keywords: mcp session, connection lifecycle, server restart, stateful server
Guidance: A stateful MCP server that loses in-memory session state on restart (with no persistence) silently breaks any in-progress multi-step tool interaction that depended on that state.
Do: Persist essential session state externally (not just in-process memory) for MCP servers expected to survive restarts or scale horizontally.
Don't: Keep all session-critical state only in server process memory with no persistence or handoff plan for restarts.

Keywords: mcp logging, stderr logging, server debugging, protocol logging
Guidance: Writing debug output to stdout on a stdio-transport server corrupts the JSON-RPC protocol stream, since stdout is the actual message channel between client and server.
Do: Log diagnostic output to stderr (never stdout) on stdio-transport MCP servers to avoid corrupting the protocol stream.
Don't: Use print() or console.log() for debug output on a stdio-transport MCP server, corrupting the JSON-RPC stream.
